184: The ambassador is unwell and will not go out for some days.
If he were less peevish and morose, all would be well.
I see only too plainly that Heaven has marked me out for severe trials; but courage — a light heart can bear anything.
I smile to find such a word coming from my pen.
A little more lightness of heart would make me the happiest creature under the sun.
But must I despair of my own talents and faculties while others of far smaller ability parade in front of me in perfect self-satisfaction?
Gracious Providence, to whom I owe all my powers, why did you not withhold some of the gifts you gave me, and put in their place a feeling of self-confidence and contentment?
185: But patience! All will yet come right; for I assure you, my dear friend, you were right.
Since I have been obliged to mix constantly with other people, and to watch what they do and how they occupy themselves, I have grown far better satisfied with myself.
For we are so made by nature that we are always inclined to compare ourselves with others, and our happiness or misery depends very much on the people and things around us.
For that reason nothing is more dangerous than solitude.
There our imagination, always ready to rise, takes a new flight on the wings of fancy and paints us a whole chain of beings among whom we seem the lowest.
Everything appears greater than it really is, and everyone seems above us.
This working of the mind is quite natural.

We feel our own imperfections so constantly, and fancy we see in others the qualities we lack, crediting them besides with everything we enjoy ourselves, that in this way we build up the idea of a perfect, happy man — a man who exists only in our own imagination.
186: But when, in spite of weakness and disappointment, we set to work in earnest and keep steadily at it, we often find that, though we have to tack the whole way, we make more headway than others who have wind and tide to help them.
And in truth there is no greater satisfaction than keeping pace with others, or outstripping them in the race.
188: I begin to find my situation here more bearable, all things considered.
I find a great advantage in having plenty to do; and the number of people I meet, and the variety of their pursuits, make an entertaining show for me.
I have made the acquaintance of the Count C—, and I think more of him every day.

He is a man of strong understanding and great discernment; and though he sees further than other people, he is not cold in his manner for all that, but capable of inspiring and returning the warmest affection.
He seemed interested in me on one occasion when I had some business to transact with him.
He saw at the first word that we understood each other, and that he could speak to me in a different tone from the one he used with others.
I cannot value his frank and open kindness to me highly enough.
It is the greatest and most genuine of pleasures to see a great mind in sympathy with our own.
190: As I expected, the ambassador causes me endless annoyance.
He is the most punctilious blockhead under heaven.
He does everything step by step, with the trifling minuteness of an old woman; and he is a man it is impossible to please, because he is never pleased with himself.
I like to do business steadily and cheerfully, and when it is finished, to leave it alone.

But he keeps sending my papers back to me, saying, "They will do" — and then recommending that I look them over again, since "one may always improve by using a better word or a more suitable particle."
At that I lose all patience and wish myself at the devil.

Not a conjunction, not an adverb may be left out; he has a deadly hatred of all those inversions I am so fond of; and if the music of a sentence is not tuned to the established official key, he cannot make out the meaning at all.
It is deplorable to be tied to such a fellow.
191: My acquaintance with the Count C— is the one compensation for such an evil.
He told me frankly the other day that he was much displeased with the ambassador's difficulties and delays, and that people like him are obstacles both to themselves and to everyone else.

"But," he added, "one must submit, like a traveller who has to climb a mountain: if the mountain were not there, the road would be both shorter and pleasanter; but there it is, and he must get over it."
192: The old man has noticed the count's partiality for me; it annoys him, and he seizes every chance to belittle the count in my hearing.
I naturally defend him, and that only makes matters worse.
Yesterday he made me indignant, for he was aiming at me as well.
"The count," he said, "is a man of the world and a good man of business: his style is good and he writes easily; but, like other geniuses, he has no solid learning."
He looked at me with an expression that seemed to ask whether I had felt the blow.
But it did not have the effect he wanted: I despise a man who can think and act in such a way.
However, I made a stand and answered with not a little warmth.
The count, I said, was a man entitled to respect, both for his character and for his attainments.

I had never met anyone whose mind was stored with more useful and wide-ranging knowledge, who had mastered such an infinite variety of subjects, and who still kept all his energy for the details of ordinary business.
This was entirely beyond him; and I took my leave, in case some new absurdity of his should rouse my anger too far.
193: And you are to blame for all this — you, who persuaded me to bend my neck to this yoke by preaching a life of activity at me.
If the man who plants vegetables and carries his corn to town on market days is not more usefully employed than I am, then let me work another ten years at the galleys I am chained to now.
194: Oh, the brilliant wretchedness, the weariness a man is doomed to witness among the silly people one meets in society here!
How they watch, how they toil, to gain precedence!
What poor and contemptible passions they display in their utter nakedness!
We have a woman here, for instance, who never stops entertaining the company with accounts of her family and her estates.

Any stranger would take her for a silly creature whose head has been turned by her pretensions to rank and property; but she is in fact even more ridiculous than that — the daughter of a mere magistrate's clerk from this neighbourhood.
I cannot understand how human beings can debase themselves so.
195: Every day I see more clearly the folly of judging others by ourselves.
And I have so much trouble with myself, and my own heart is in such constant agitation, that I am quite content to let others go their own way, if they will only allow me the same.
196: What provokes me most is the wretched lengths to which distinctions of rank are carried.
I know perfectly well how necessary inequalities of condition are, and I am aware of the advantages I draw from them myself.
But I would rather these institutions did not stand in the way of the small chance of happiness I might enjoy on this earth.
197: I have lately got to know a Miss B—, a very agreeable girl who has kept her natural manners in the middle of an artificial life.
Our first conversation pleased us both equally; and when I took my leave I asked permission to visit her.
She agreed so obligingly that I waited impatiently for the happy moment to arrive.
She is not a native of this place, but lives here with her aunt.
The old lady's face is not prepossessing.
I paid her a great deal of attention, addressing most of my conversation to her; and in less than half an hour I had discovered what her niece afterwards admitted to me.

Her aged aunt, having but a small fortune and a still smaller share of understanding, takes no satisfaction in anything but the pedigree of her ancestors, seeks no protection but her noble birth, and enjoys nothing but looking out from her castle over the heads of the humble townspeople.
She was no doubt handsome in her youth, and in her early years probably trifled her time away making many a poor young man the sport of her caprice.
In her riper years she submitted to the yoke of a veteran officer who, in return for her person and her small independence, spent with her what we may call her age of brass.
He is dead, and she is now a widow, and deserted.
She spends her iron age alone, and nobody would come near her, were it not for the loveliness of her niece.
199: What creatures men are, whose whole thoughts are taken up with form and ceremony, who devote years of mental and physical effort to the task of advancing themselves a single step and getting a higher place at the table.
Not that such people would otherwise be short of occupation — on the contrary, they make a great deal of trouble for themselves by neglecting important business for such petty trifles.
Last week a question of precedence arose at a sledging party, and spoiled all our amusement.
200: The silly creatures cannot see that it is not place that makes real greatness, since the man who occupies the first place seldom plays the principal part.
How many kings are governed by their ministers — how many ministers by their secretaries?
Who, in such cases, is really the chief?
The man, it seems to me, who can see through the rest, and who has strength or skill enough to make their power or their passions serve his own designs.
202: I must write to you from this place, my dear Charlotte — from a small room in a country inn, where I have taken shelter from a severe storm.
During my whole stay in that wretched town of D—, where I lived among strangers, strangers indeed to this heart, I never once felt the least inclination to write to you.
But in this cottage, in this retirement, in this solitude, with the snow and hail beating against my window, you are my first thought.
The instant I came in, your figure rose before me, and the memory of you!
O my Charlotte, the sacred, tender memory!
Gracious Heaven, give me back the happy moment when we first met.
203: Could you but see me, my dear Charlotte, in this whirl of dissipation — how my senses are dried up, and my heart never once full.
I do not enjoy a single moment of happiness: everything is empty, nothing touches me.
I stand as if before a peep-show: I watch the little puppets move, and ask myself whether it is not all an optical illusion.
I am amused by these puppets — or rather I am one of them myself; but when I sometimes take my neighbour's hand, I feel it is not a natural thing, and draw mine back with a shudder.
In the evening I say I will enjoy tomorrow's sunrise, and yet I stay in bed; in the day I promise myself a walk by moonlight, and yet I stay at home.
I do not know why I get up, nor why I go to sleep.
204: The leaven that gave my life its rise is gone.
The charm that cheered me in the gloom of the night, and roused me out of my sleep in the morning, has fled for ever.
205: I have found only one person here to interest me, a Miss B—.
She is like you, my dear Charlotte, if anyone can possibly be like you.
"Ah!" you will say, "he has learned how to pay fine compliments."
I have been very agreeable lately, since it was not in my power to be otherwise.
I have a good deal of wit besides; and the ladies say that nobody understands flattery better — or falsehood, you will add, since the one accomplishment always goes with the other.
But I must tell you about Miss B—.
She has an abundance of soul, which flashes out of her deep blue eyes.
Her rank is a torment to her, and satisfies not one desire of her heart.
She would gladly retire from this whirl of fashion, and we often picture to ourselves a life of undisturbed happiness somewhere far off in the country.
And then we speak of you, my dear Charlotte; for she knows you and pays homage to your merits — homage that is not demanded of her but freely given.
She loves you, and delights to hear you made the subject of conversation.
206: Oh, that I were sitting at your feet in your favourite little room, with the dear children playing around us!
If they became troublesome to you, I would tell them some appalling goblin story, and they would crowd round me in silent attention.
The sun is setting in glory; his last rays are shining on the snow that covers the face of the country.
The storm is over, and I must go back to my dungeon.
Adieu! Is Albert with you? And what is he to you?
208: For a week past we have had the most wretched weather; but for me it is a blessing.
Since I came here, not one fine day has shone out of the heavens without being spoiled for me by somebody's intrusion.
In the worst of the rain and sleet and frost and storm, I congratulate myself that it cannot be worse indoors than out, nor worse out of doors than it is within — and so I am reconciled.
When the sun rises bright in the morning and promises a glorious day, I never fail to exclaim: "There, now, they have another blessing from Heaven, and they will be sure to destroy it."
"They spoil everything — health, fame, happiness, amusement; and generally they do it through folly, ignorance, or imbecility, and always, by their own account, with the best intentions."
I could often beg them on my knees to be less determined on their own destruction.
210: I fear my ambassador and I shall not stay together much longer.
He is really growing past endurance.
He conducts his business in so ridiculous a manner that I am often compelled to contradict him and do things my own way; and then of course he thinks them very badly done.
He complained of me lately on this account at court, and the minister gave me a reprimand — a gentle one, it is true, but still a reprimand.
I was on the point of tendering my resignation when I received a letter from him, to which I submitted with great respect, on account of the high, noble, and generous spirit that dictated it.
He tried to soothe my excessive sensibility, and paid a tribute to my extreme ideas of duty, of good example, and of perseverance in business, as the fruit of my youthful ardour.
It was an impulse, he said, that he did not wish to destroy but only to moderate, so that it might have proper play and be productive of good.
So now I am at peace for another week, and no longer at odds with myself.
Contentment and peace of mind are valuable things; I could wish, my dear friend, that these precious jewels were less fleeting.
212: God bless you, my dear friends, and may he grant you the happiness he denies to me.
213: I thank you, Albert, for having deceived me.
I waited for the news that your wedding day was fixed; and I intended on that day, with all solemnity, to take Charlotte's profile down from the wall and bury it with some other papers I have.
You are now united, and her picture is still hanging here.
I know that I am still one of your circle, that I still hold an unspoiled place in Charlotte's heart, that I hold the second place there; and I mean to keep it.
Oh, I should go mad if she could forget!
Farewell, Albert; farewell, angel of heaven; farewell, Charlotte!
